paragraphs.text:
GREGORY, PRESBYTER OF ANTIOCH
On the [?] "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

1. This affectionate father (54), out of his affection for us, has sent me the theme of my discourse. He has repaid with this present address the praise you offered him on my account, for he counts the benefit of his children as his own gain. I gladly accepted his encouragement, and with confidence I raise my voice among you once again. I am eager to give you the continuation of my earlier discourse, as you wish. On the previous Sunday I showed you Christ coming to baptism together with his servants. Then I showed you the Baptist recognizing the Master who had come to him, and declining to give baptism to the one who had given baptism, but afterward carrying out the ministry of the divine plan at the Saviour's command. I described the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ crying out from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." When I had reached this testimony I came down from the pulpit, because the hour had cut short the course of my discourse. So today I want to take up again what I was forced to leave off then for lack of time. I want to join the chain back onto the discourse, so that you may hold fast to it and climb up by it to the one who forged it.

2. "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." This is he who, together with me, sent the Holy Spirit upon himself, and who in turn received the Spirit he had sent. This is he who was begotten of me before all ages: begotten, not created; begotten, not appointed; a Son begotten of me alone, only-begotten, begotten in a manner that is his alone, as I alone know and as he alone understands. This is the perfect imprint of my perfection. This is he who expresses my Godhead in

himself. This is he who clearly reproduces the image of my being. He is my Son, not a stranger. He is my Son, who shone forth from my essence without body, without flux and without time, and did not emerge from some other being. He is my Son by nature, not by grace. He is my Son, coeternal with me: not younger, not second, not added later. He is my Son, of one essence with me, not of another essence. He is of one essence with me as light from light, as life from life, as spring from spring, as truth from truth, as power from power, as God from God. I begot, he was begotten, and between me and him there is nothing. I begot as it befitted me to beget, since I am God by nature. He was begotten as it befitted him to be begotten, since he is God the Word. The word "begetting" is a human one, but the offspring that is beyond time is a mystery. Time does not know the mystery of my begetting, for time did not yet exist. The angels do not know it, for they came into being after it.

3. The Cherubim and the Seraphim, with their many eyes and many faces, cover their faces with their wings as with hands and cry out unceasingly: "Holy, holy, holy, Lord of Sabaoth." They do not say, "Holy, holier, holiest." They do not build a ladder of Godhead with a lower rung, a slightly higher one, and then a supreme one (55). They do not cut the one [?] into unequal principles. They do not make doctrines about what they do not see. They sing hymns to the one they revere; they do not pry into him. They worship the Godhead of the Trinity; they do not audit it. They offer equal hymns to me and to my Son. Their life is a hymn that asks no questions, and their existence is an untroubled melody. The heavens declare the glory of the God who made them; they do not search out the essence of their Maker. The heavens declare his glory by being seen, not by speaking. The prophets could not grasp the one who cannot be grasped, for all human nature is too weak to comprehend him. The mind cannot contain the one who cannot be contained. Reason cannot encompass God made man. Faith alone perceives the one who cannot be seen. Faith alone draws near to the one who cannot be approached, as far as is possible, and as far as [?]

4. "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." This is my fellow worker, not my underling. This one made heaven and earth. This one curved the circle of the firmament above, smoothed it below, and spread it out. This one adorned the visible face of the sky with stars as with eyes. This one made the sun the leader and general of the day. This one yoked to the gloom of night the brightness of the moon, which chases away the dejection of the night. This one poured out the soft nature of the air, which is easily breathed by those who live in it, which parts readily around the faces of those who walk through it, and which closes again painlessly behind

their backs. This one placed the seeds of fruits in the flanks of the earth, casting down his command like a seed, and crowned the face of the earth with countless plants and flowers. This one fixed the fine sand as a boundary between land and sea. When the sea sees it, it stays within its own bounds, not daring to pass beyond them or to encroach on the neighbouring land. This one fashioned the turning of the seasons, the changes of the times, and the unfailing succession of the years. This one established the visible and the invisible creation. He did not need time to help him, nor was he enslaved to toil and labour. He only willed, and brought all things forth with ease. He nodded, and his nod became substance for the things that exist. He only thought, and the thought became a deed [?]. He called the things that are not as though they were, and all things, as if they already existed and were his servants, came running together at their Master's call. This is he to whom I said in counsel: "Let us make man in our image and after our likeness." This is he who formed man together with me, and who for man's sake became man without being changed into man. He became man without being transformed into what he became. He became man by taking up the firstfruits of humanity, not by casting off the lightning-flash of the Godhead. He became man and remained God.

5. This is he who was never separated from my bosom, and yet took up his place in the womb of Mary. He remains in me inseparably, and came to be in her without being confined. He exists in the heavens undivided, and dwelt in the virgin womb undefiled; for he was not defiled in creating that womb, and he was not stained by dwelling in it. This is he who came forth from a blessed womb like a radiant bridegroom from a bridal chamber that knew no marriage. By his birth he honoured the birth of those born of earth, and by being born he set a seal on the virginity of the woman who bore him. He entered the world, which he had never left, through the gates of virginity, and did not break the bolts of the gates of purity. He was carried by his mother, and he carries all things. He needed milk as an infant, and he nourishes all creation as its Nourisher. He was wrapped in a baby's swaddling clothes as a child, and as God he loosens the swaddling bands of sins. He lay in a manger, and was pointed out by a star as the Creator of the stars. He was warred against by Herod, and was hailed as Lord by Simeon, prophet and priest. He went down to Egypt, shook the handmade idols of Egypt, and fulfilled my prophecy that says: "Out of Egypt I called my Son." He grew in bodily stature but not in divine essence, for where could one who is present everywhere grow? He was baptized by the Baptist, and he enlightened creation.

6. "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." My Son is not one person and the Son of Mary another. The one laid in the cave is not one person and the one worshipped by the Magi another

Gen. 1:26. Hos. 11:1.

[?] baptized. No, this is my Son. This is the one who is both perceived by the mind and seen, the one who is invisible and yet seen by you, the one who is eternal and yet in time. He is the same one who is of one essence with me in his Godhead, and of one essence with you in his humanity, in all things apart from sin. Do not look on earth for a father of his flesh, for below he has no father. Do not look in heaven for a mother of his Godhead, for above he has no mother. Do not divide his Godhead from his humanity. Do not become wicked dividers of what cannot be divided. Do not separate his humanity from his Godhead, for after the union it is undivided and unconfused. Do not separate what is in him; rather, recognize what is in him. Do not make the one person of Christ into two persons. Do not appoint the one Only-begotten as two only-begottens. Do not set my Son on one side and what he assumed on the other. Do not dare to divide the unconfused union, which cannot be divided. Do not suppose that the Lord who became man is either God stripped bare or a mere man. Rather, believe that the same one is God and man at once. He always existed and existed beforehand as God, but he was not always also man; he became man, and is man, from the moment when, by his own will, he took hold of the seed of Abraham.

7. If you see this Son of mine hungry, or thirsty, or sleeping, or walking, or weary, or being scourged, or crucified willingly, or held by the nails by his own choice, or put to death by his own will, or guarded as a corpse in a tomb, attribute these things to his flesh [?]. And again, if you see this Son of mine scraping away leprosy with a word, healing blind eyes with clay, shaping nature with a nod, feeding five thousand from five loaves, and raising in the palms of his disciples, as in fields, an instant and unsown harvest; if you see him calming with his voice the raging sea that was mimicking the mountain peaks, walking on the deep as on solid ground, and giving orders to demons as a master to slaves, attribute these things to his Godhead. Do not think that the lofty deeds belong to one person and the lowly events to another. Count both the one and the other as belonging to one and the same person. All that is divine is his, all that is human is his; the works of creation are his, and the sufferings are his. For my Son is one and the same: he performs the works of his own Godhead, and he makes his own everything that belongs to his flesh.

"This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." This is the vine, and the door for the sheep that had been straying until now. He is a vine with its root in heaven and its branches on earth; a vine pruned in its body but not withered in its root; a vine that, on the third day after its pruning, puts forth the cluster of the resurrection. This is the door, for through him the believer comes in to me. This is the mediator between me and his servants, for in himself he joins to me those who had offended.

This [?] is my Son and the Lamb. He is priest and victim; the same one offers and is offered; the same one becomes the sacrifice and himself receives the sacrifice (56).

8. This, then, is the testimony the Father gave concerning the Only-begotten after the baptism at the Jordan. And when Christ was transfigured on the mountain while the disciples watched, and his face sent out rays that eclipsed the rays of the sun, then too the Father uttered the same words again: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." The Father often calls the Son "Son", and with his voice he holds fast the Only-begotten as with a hand. He does so because of those who say that the timeless one was born in time, because of those who count the Maker of creation among the creatures, because of those who make a slave of the Liberator, and because of those who invent one son and then another. That is why he bears witness again and again: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him." If he says, "I am in the Father and the Father is in me," listen to him. If he says, "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father," listen to him, for his words are borne out by the facts. If he says, "The Father who sent me is greater than I," apply the saying to the divine plan of his condescension. If he says, "This is my body, broken for you for the forgiveness of sins" (57), look at the body he shows you. Look at what was taken from you, became his own, and is broken for you. If he says, "This is my blood," consider it the blood of the one who is speaking to you, and of no one else besides him. If he says, "My soul is sorrowful even to death," attribute the suffering of sorrow to his soul.

9. These things we have been taught by God the Father. These things we have been instructed in by the only-begotten Son of God. These things have been declared by the holy Scriptures. These things have been proclaimed by the holy Fathers. So let us guard what we have received, and hold fast to what we have learned. Why do we fight one another for nothing? Why do we make war on one another, we who are commanded to love even those who hate us? Why do we abandon believing and turn the faith into technical argument? "He was born"; "He was not born." "He suffered"; "He did not suffer." "He rose"; "He did not rise." Why do we take the Redeemer to court? Why do we audit the

[?] again to judge the living and the dead. Then Judas will see whom he sold to the killers of the Lord, and the Jews will see what kind of head they crowned with thorns. When they see him seated on the judgment throne, with the Cherubim standing by in fear and trembling, they will say, "We did not crucify this one; we condemned a certain Jesus, a Nazarene from Bethlehem." Then he will show them his side, and they will look on him whom they pierced, and they will worship him even against their will.

10. (39) [Why then do we abandon believing and turn the faith into technical argument? Why do we fulfil the desire of our common enemy? The devil, the common destroyer of humanity, reckoned as follows: when calm prevails among us, piety flourishes; when faith shines (40), good living prevails; and when we achieve a God-loving way of life, with blessedness as our mediator (41), we become friends of the Creator and run back up to the one we long for (42). So, to keep us from ascending (43) to the place from which he fell, see what he has done! See how cunningly and deceitfully (44) he has stitched together a war against us, this contriver of evils, wise in deceits, intricate in plots, and rich in wicked devices! He has prepared (45) certain people to campaign under the pretext of piety. He has armed (46) inquiry into the faith against the faith itself. Through them he has launched against all the pious an untimely and soul-destroying war of contention, and he has set the members of the Church to fight one another. Then he laughs a broad laugh as he watches his followers delighting in his counsels, and delighting him by what they do against one another, without stopping even after they have experienced the evils it brings. So let us turn this cleverness of his back upon the evil one's own head. Let us change his merriment into grief and inconsolable mourning, and let us long for the peace that he hates. Let us stop weighing (48) and measuring the words of doctrine. Let us stop wanting to be teachers of our teachers. Let us hate battles over words that ruin those who hear them. Let us believe as our Fathers handed down. We are not wiser than the Fathers. We are not more precise than our teachers. We are not shepherds of the shepherds, but sheep; and the sheep do not shepherd the shepherds, but the shepherds the sheep. God has called (50) us in peace (49), not in battle; as we were called, so let us remain. Let us shudder (51) before the mystical

(40) [?] Ed. κρατούσης. (45) Ed., less well, ἐπέλθωμεν. (45) Ed. παρασκευάζει. (48) Ed. ζυγομαχεῖν. (50) Ed. ἐκάλεσεν. (51) Ed. προσμείνωμεν.

table at which we partake of the heavenly mysteries (52). Let us not be table companions and plotters against one another at the same time (53). Let us not be in communion here and quarrelsome outside (54)]. Let us not share one faith here and side with others outside. Otherwise the Lord may say of us too: "I begot sons and raised them up, and nourished them from my own flesh, but they rejected me." May the Saviour of all, the Creator of peace, himself drive away from you the devil, who loves disorder and war. May he himself grant calm to his Churches. May he himself keep this holy flock safe. May he himself protect its chief shepherd. May he himself guard our pious and Christ-loving emperor. May he himself gather the straying sheep into his folds, so that there may be one flock and one fold. To him be glory and power to the ages of ages. Amen.
